newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX electrics hit new highs, traders perplexed.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX electrics hit new highs, traders perplexed.

text.p: NYMEX electricity futures unexpectedly surged Tuesday to new levels in a move that was so strong it left many traders perplexed as to the reason for the jump, industry sources said.

"I want to say I don't know what happened, but it's probably a combination of factors," said one Houston-based futures trader, adding upward pressure was seen from Southwestern cooling demand, generation unit outages, and strong physical power prices.
"There may have been a few people caught in a squeeze," said another futures trader.

NYMEX June Palo Verde (PV) ended up $3.73 at $29.81 per megawatt hour (MWh) after hitting a new contract high of $31.00 and trading as low as $27.00, while July ended up $2.70 at $30.50 from trade at a new contract high of $31.50 and a low of $29.00 per MWh.
Remaining PV deferreds finished up between 50 cents and $2.63 per MWh.

June California Oregon Border (COB) closed up $3.01 at $22.41 after hitting a new high of $23.00 and trade as low as $20.00, while July finished up $2.16 at a new contract high of $22.25 and trade as low as $20.00 per MWh.
Remaining COB deferreds closed up between 60 cents and $2.68 per MWh.

The futures climbed despite only slightly higher to weaker physical power prices in the West, where peak, firm COB for Wednesday delivery was talked at $24.50-26.00 earlier today from $24.00-25.50 for Tuesday delivery.
Firm, peak PV electricity for Wednesday fell to $30.00-35.00 from $34.00-38.00 for today, sources said.
Sources said it remained to be seen whether the power futures could maintain the new levels.
"The last time we hit these levels in December and January we lost that strength, but this time we may be able to hold it," said the Houston-based trader.
Contract volumes were not immediately available from NYMEX.
NYMEX June Henry Hub electricity futures finished down 2.4 cents at $2.191 per million British thermal units.

Separately, at least 7,000 megawatts of power remained off line in the West for either planned or unplanned maintenance, although a significant portion was expected to return to service over the next several weeks.

As part of the service resumptions, Pacific Gas & Electric's 1,087 megawatt Diablo Canyon 1 was scheduled to begin production May 25 following a scheduled refueling and maintenance outage which began April 19.

Although the California Coast are expected to see mild spring readings in the 70s degree Fahrenheit, interior sections of the Southwest were forecast to continue experiencing temperatures in the 90-100 degree range into next week.

In the Pacific Northwest, temperatures were expected to average near normal in the northeast to two degrees above normal in the southwest over the next several days, with a few scattered showers likely in the north.
